nodes.name: Classical Bernstein operator
nodes.statement: It is well known that the classical Bernstein operator $B_{n}: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\},$ defined by \begin{equation} B_{n}f\left( x\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( \frac{k}{n}\right) \binom{n}{k} x^{k}\left( 1-x\right) ^{n-k} \end{equation} has good shape preserving properties, a fact that explains its usefulness in computer assisted geometric design.
nodes.statement_short: The classical Bernstein operator $B_n f(x)=\sum_k f(k/n)\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k}$, with good shape-preserving properties.

nodes.name: Bernstein operator formula
nodes.statement: B_{n}f\left( x\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( \frac{k}{n}\right) \binom{n}{k} x^{k}\left( 1-x\right) ^{n-k}
nodes.label: defBP

nodes.name: Berens-DeVore extremal property of Bernstein polynomials
nodes.statement: In \cite{BeVo}, Berens and DeVore consider operators $L_n: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\},$ fixing $1$ and $x$, and such that $(L_nf)^{(j)}\geq 0$ if $f^{(j)}\geq 0$ for $j=0,1,2,\cdots,n$. They show that for every $n$, $L_n x^2 \ge B_n x^2$, and if for some $t\in (0,1)$, $L_n t^2 = B_n t^2$, then $L_n \equiv B_n$.
assumptions: operators $L_n: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\},$ fixing $1$ and $x$, and such that $(L_nf)^{(j)}\geq 0$ if $f^{(j)}\geq 0$ for $j=0,1,2,\cdots,n$
for some $t\in (0,1)$, $L_n t^2 = B_n t^2$
conclusions: for every $n$, $L_n x^2 \ge B_n x^2$
if for some $t\in (0,1)$, $L_n t^2 = B_n t^2$, then $L_n \equiv B_n$

assumptions: for some $t\in (0,1)$, $L_n t^2 = B_n t^2$
conclusions: $L_n \equiv B_n$

nodes.statement_short: Shape-preserving polynomial operators fixing 1 and x satisfy $L_n x^2\ge B_n x^2$, with equality at one interior point forcing $L_n=B_n$.

nodes.name: Positive measures mu_{n,k}
nodes.statement: For each pair $n,k$ of nonnegative integers, let $\mu_{n,k}$ be a positive measure.

nodes.name: Bernstein basis polynomials
nodes.statement: Denote by $p_{n,k} (x) := \binom{n}{k} x^{k}\left( 1-x\right) ^{n-k}$ the elements of the Bernstein basis for the space of polynomials.

nodes.name: Class L_n of positive linear operators
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal L_n$ be the class of positive linear operators $L_n: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\}$ fixing $1$ and $x$ (so $L_n$ preserves affine functions) and defined by \begin{equation} L_n f (x) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} \lambda_{n,k}(f) p_{n, k} (x), \ \ \ \ \mbox{ where } \ \ \ \ \lambda_{n,k}(f) := \int_0^1 f d \mu_{n,k}. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: class of positive linear operators $L_n: C\left[ 0,1\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{Span}\{1, x, \dots, x^n\}$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal L_n$: positive linear operators into degree-$n$ polynomials fixing 1 and $x$, of the form $\sum_k \lambda_{n,k}(f)p_{n,k}$ with $\lambda_{n,k}(f)=\int f d\mu_{n,k}$.

nodes.name: Operators L_n via measures
nodes.statement: L_n f (x) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} \lambda_{n,k}(f) p_{n, k} (x), \ \ \ \ \mbox{ where } \ \ \ \ \lambda_{n,k}(f) := \int_0^1 f d \mu_{n,k}.
nodes.label: defl

nodes.name: Dirac delta probability
nodes.statement: Denote by $\delta_x$ the Dirac delta probability, which assigns mass 1 to the singleton $\{x\}$, and observe that $B_n\in \mathcal L_n$ is obtained by taking $\mu_{n,k} = \delta_{k/n}$ in (\ref{defl}), so $\lambda_{n,k}(f) = f(k/n)$.

nodes.name: Bernstein operator dominates convex functions
nodes.statement: Recall that if $\phi$ is convex on $[0,1]$, then $B_n\phi \ge \phi$ on that interval.
assumptions: $\phi$ is convex on $[0,1]$
conclusions: $B_n\phi \ge \phi$ on that interval

nodes.name: Optimality of Bernstein operators for convex functions
nodes.statement: From \cite[Theorem 1]{BuQue} and the generalization in \cite[Theorem 2]{CC}, it is known that $L_n\phi \ge B_n\phi$ for every convex function $\phi$ and every $L_n \in \mathcal L_n$, and furthermore, $L_n\equiv B_n$ if $L_n\psi (t) = B_n\psi (t)$ for some strictly convex function $\psi$ and some $t\in (0,1)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Bustamante & Quesada 2006; de la Cal & Carcamo 2007
assumptions: every $L_n \in \mathcal L_n$
$L_n\psi (t) = B_n\psi (t)$ for some strictly convex function $\psi$ and some $t\in (0,1)$
conclusions: $L_n\phi \ge B_n\phi$ for every convex function $\phi$
$L_n\equiv B_n$

nodes.statement_short: Every $L_n\in\mathcal L_n$ satisfies $L_n\phi\ge B_n\phi$ on convex $\phi$; equality at one point for a strictly convex function forces $L_n=B_n$.

nodes.name: Fixing 1 and x forces probability measures with mean k/n
nodes.statement: Observe that by uniqueness of the coefficients of the basis functions, the condition $L_n 1 \equiv 1$ entails that each $\mu_{n,k}$ is a probability measure, while $L_n x \equiv x$ entails that the expectation of $x$ with respect to $\mu_{n,k}$ is $\int_0^1 x d \mu_{n,k} (x) = k/n$.
nodes.statement_short: $L_n1=1$ makes each $\mu_{n,k}$ a probability measure; $L_nx=x$ makes its mean $k/n$.

nodes.name: Dropping the condition L_n x = x
nodes.statement: If the assumption $L_n x \equiv x$ is dropped, then the resulting operator may fail to preserve convexity, and may approximate some convex functions better than $B_n$ (while in other cases the approximation will be worse, notably for $x$ itself).

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator B_{n,j} fixing 1 and x^j
nodes.statement: {\rm Let $1 < j \le n$. In \cite[Proposition 11]{AKR3} and in \cite[Example 5.3]{Mazu09}, a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ fixing $1$ and $x^{j}$, is defined by \begin{equation*} \mathcal{B}_{n,j}f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( \left[ \frac{k(k-1)\cdots (k-j+1)}{ n(n-1)\cdots (n-j+1)}\right] ^{1/j}\right) \binom{n}{k}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}. \end{equation*} In particular, if $j = 1$ this is the classical Bernstein operator. However, for $j > 1$ and all $k = 1, 2, \dots$, $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k < B_{n} x^k$ on $(0,1)$, since the operator $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ samples the strictly increasing functions $x^k$ at nodes lower than those of $B_{n}$ (except the first and the last nodes, which are 0 and 1 in both cases). It is shown in \cite[Example 17]{AKR3} that if $1\le k\le j$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \le x^k$, while if $j\le k$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \ge x^k$. Hence, on $(0,1)$, ${B}_{n} x^k > \mathcal{B}_{n,j} x^k \ge x^k$ when $j\le k$. Of course, $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ does not preserve convexity, since $$ \mathcal{B}_{n,j} (1 - x) = \mathcal{B}_{n,j}(1) -\mathcal{B}_{n,j}( x) > 1- B_n (x) = 1 - x $$ whenever $x\in (0,1)$. But $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ does preserve $(1,x^j)$-convexity, defined below.}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}$ fixes 1 and $x^j$, approximates $x^k$ better than $B_n$ for $k\ge j$, but fails to preserve convexity while preserving $(1,x^j)$-convexity.
nodes.label: ex1

nodes.name: Extended Chebyshev space
nodes.statement: An \emph{extended Chebyshev space} $U_{n}$ of dimension $n+1$ over the interval $\left[ a,b\right] $ is an $n+1$ dimensional subspace of $C^{n}\left( \left[a,b\right] \right)$ such that each function $f\in U_{n}$ not vanishing identically, has at most $n$ zeros in $\left[ a,b\right]$, counting multiplicities.
differentia: each function $f\in U_{n}$ not vanishing identically, has at most $n$ zeros in $\left[ a,b\right]$, counting multiplicities

nodes.name: Non-negative Bernstein basis
nodes.statement: It is well-known that extended Chebyshev spaces possess \emph{non-negative Bernstein bases}, i.e. collections of non-negative functions $p_{n,k},k=0,...,n,$ in $U_{n}$, such that each $p_{n,k}$ has a zero of order $k$ at $a$ and a zero of order $n-k$ at $b$, for $k=0,...,n$.
differentia: each $p_{n,k}$ has a zero of order $k$ at $a$ and a zero of order $n-k$ at $b$

nodes.name: Fixed functions f_0, f_1
nodes.statement: Now let us select two functions $f_{0},f_{1}\in U_{n},$ such that $f_{0} >0 $ and $f_{1}/f_{0}$ is strictly increasing (these functions play the role of 1 and $x$ in the classical case).

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator
nodes.statement: It is sometimes possible to define a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}:C\left[ a,b\right] \rightarrow U_{n}$ fixing $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$, by first suitably choosing nodes $t_{n,0},...,t_{n,n}\in \left[ a,b\right]$ such that $t_{n,0} = a$ and $t_{n,n}= b$, second, by selecting appropriate weights $\alpha _{n,0},...,\alpha _{n,n} > 0$, and finally, by setting \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( t_{n,k}\right) \alpha _{n,k}p_{n,k}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{B}_n f=\sum_k f(t_{n,k})\alpha_{n,k}p_{n,k}$ with nodes $t_{n,0}=a,\dots,t_{n,n}=b$ and positive weights, fixing $f_0,f_1$.

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator with weights
nodes.statement: \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( t_{n,k}\right) \alpha _{n,k}p_{n,k}.
nodes.label: eqBern

nodes.name: Relabelled basis absorbing the weights
nodes.statement: For simplicity in the notation, we relabel the basis functions so that they already incorporate the weights $\alpha _{n,k}$. Thus, (\ref{eqBern}) becomes \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( t_{n,k}\right) p_{n,k}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operator, relabelled
nodes.statement: \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}f\left( t_{n,k}\right) p_{n,k}.
nodes.label: eqber

nodes.name: Standing assumption on f_0 and f_1
nodes.statement: The functions $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ are always assumed to satisfy the conditions ``$f_{0} >0$" and ``$f_{1}/f_{0}$ is strictly increasing".

nodes.name: Existence and non-existence of generalized Bernstein operators
nodes.statement: {\rm Given an extended Chebyshev space $U_n$, it is always possible to {\em select} some pair $f_0$ and $f_1$ in $U_n$ for which a generalized Bernstein operator can be defined (cf. \cite[Corollary 8]{AKR3}). However, for some choices of $f_0$ and $f_1$, $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ may fail to exist. For instance, it is well known that if $0 < b < 2\pi$, then $U_3 :=\operatorname{Span} \{1,x, \cos x, \sin x\}$ on the interval $[0,b]$ is an extended Chebyshev space. But there is no generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixing $1$ and $x$ if $b=5$ (for instance) while such $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ does exist if $b = 4$, cf. \cite[Theorem 25]{AKR3}.}
nodes.statement_short: Some pair $f_0,f_1$ always admits a generalized Bernstein operator, but not every pair: for Span$\{1,x,\cos x,\sin x\}$ on $[0,b]$ none fixing 1, x exists if $b=5$.

nodes.name: Endpoint interpolation of generalized Bernstein operators
nodes.statement: {\rm The condition on the zeros of $p_{n,k}$ entails that, like the classical Bernstein operator, the operators given by (\ref{eqBern}) interpolate functions at the endpoints of the interval $[a,b]$: Since $f_0$ is strictly positive, from $f_0 (a) = \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f_0\right) (a) = f_0\left( a\right) \alpha _{n, 0}p_{n,0} (a)$ we conclude that $\alpha _{n, 0}p_{n,0} (a) = 1$. Likewise, $\alpha_{n, n}p_{n,n} (b) = 1$, so we always have $\mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) (a) = f(a)$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n}\left( f\right) (b) = f(b)$.}
nodes.statement_short: Generalized Bernstein operators interpolate at the endpoints $a$ and $b$.
nodes.label: interp

nodes.name: Convexity via affine interpolation
nodes.statement: Convexity of $\phi$ can be defined by saying that if we interpolate between $\phi (x)$ and $\phi(y)$ using an affine function $h$, then on $[x,y]$ the graph of $\phi$ lies below the graph of $h$.

nodes.name: (f_0, f_1)-convexity
nodes.statement: If instead of affine functions we use $(f_0, f_1)$-affine functions, that is, functions in $\operatorname{Span} \{f_0, f_1\}$, we obtain the corresponding notion of {\em $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity}.
nodes.statement_short: Convexity where interpolation uses functions in Span$\{f_0,f_1\}$ instead of affine functions.

nodes.name: Strict (f_0, f_1)-convexity
nodes.statement: Strict $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity is defined analogously to strict convexity.

nodes.name: Generalized Bernstein operators preserve (f_0,f_1)-convexity
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite[Theorem 22]{AKR3} (cf. also \cite[Proposition 4.14]{Mazu09}) that a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixing $f_0$ and $f_1$ preserves $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity.
assumptions: a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixing $f_0$ and $f_1$
conclusions: preserves $(f_0, f_1)$-convexity

nodes.name: Bessenyei-Pales characterization of (f_0,f_1)-convexity
nodes.statement: Let $I:= (f_1/f_0)([a,b])$. Then $\phi\in C[a,b]$ is $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\phi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is convex in the standard sense.
assumptions: $\phi\in C[a,b]$
conclusions: $\phi\in C[a,b]$ is $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\phi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is convex in the standard sense
equivalent_conditions: $(\phi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is convex in the standard sense
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is $(f_0,f_1)$-convex iff $(\phi/f_0)\circ(f_1/f_0)^{-1}$ is convex.
nodes.label: bepa

nodes.name: Case f_0 = 1 is a change of variables
nodes.statement: In particular, if $f_0 = 1$, the relationship between convexity and $(1, f_1)$-convexity is given by a simple change of variables (determined by $f_1$).

nodes.name: Monomials x^k and (1,x^j)-convexity
nodes.statement: For instance, returning to Example \ref{ex1}, and to the functions considered there, we see that if $1 \le k \le j$, then $x^k$ is $(1, x^j)$-concave, while if $j \le k \le n$, then $x^k$ is $(1, x^j)$-convex.

nodes.statement: It is entirely analogous to Theorem \ref{bepa}, save that strict convexity replaces convexity throughout. The proof is also essentially the same, and thus we omit it. Basically, all one needs to do is to use strict inequalities $>$ instead of $\ge$, at the appropriate places.

nodes.name: Strict version of the Bessenyei-Pales characterization
nodes.statement: Let $I:= (f_1/f_0)([a,b])$. Then $\psi\in C[a,b]$ is strictly $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\psi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is strictly convex.

conclusions: $\psi\in C[a,b]$ is strictly $(f_0, f_1)$-convex if and only if $(\psi/f_0) \circ (f_1/f_0)^{-1} \in C\left(I\right)$ is strictly convex

nodes.name: Optimality of generalized Bernstein operators
nodes.statement: Let $U_{n}\subset C^{n}\left[ a,b\right]$ be an extended Chebyshev space containing the functions $f_0$ and $f_1$, with $f_0 > 0$ and $f_1/f_0$ strictly increasing. Suppose there exists a generalized Bernstein operator $\mathcal{B}_{n}:C\left[ a,b\right] \rightarrow U_{n}$ fixing $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$. Let the operator $L_{n}:C\left[ a,b\right] \rightarrow U_{n}$, subject to $L_n f_0 = f_0$ and $L_n f_1 = f_1$, be defined by \begin{equation} L_{n}\left( f\right) =\sum_{k=0}^{n}\lambda_{n,k} (f) p_{n,k}, \end{equation} where $p_{n,k}$ has the same meaning as in (\ref{eqber}), and $\lambda_{n,k}(f) $ is obtained from $f$ and the positive measure $\mu_{n,k}$ via \begin{equation} \lambda_{n, k}(f) := f_0 (t_{n,k}) \int_a^b f d \mu_{n,k}. \end{equation} Then, for every $(f_0, f_1)$-convex function $\phi$, we have $\phi\le \mathcal{B}_{n} \phi \le L_n \phi$. Moreover, if for some $t\in (a,b)$ and some strictly $(f_0, f_1)$-convex function $\psi$ we have $\mathcal{B}_{n} \psi (t) = L_n \psi (t)$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n} \equiv L_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: Recall from (\ref{exponen}) that $\mu_0 = \lambda_0$ and $\mu_1 = \lambda_n$. Using (\ref{bopmone}), (\ref{basisMN}), and (\ref{eqphin}), we obtain \[ \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{0}x}\right) = e^{\lambda_{0}x} \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\left( \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k} =e^{\lambda_{0}x} \left(\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) + 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n} =e^{\lambda_{0}x}. \] Furthermore, \begin{align*} \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{n}x}\right) & = \sum_{k=0}^{n} e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\left( \lambda_{n}-\lambda_{0}\right) \frac{k}{n}\left( b-a\right) }e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) } \binom{n}{k}\left( \varphi _{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom {n}{k}\left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{k}\left( 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n-k}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\left( e^{\omega _{n}\left( b-a\right) }\varphi_{n} \left( x\right) + 1-\varphi_{n}\left( x\right) \right) ^{n}\\ & = e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }\left( \left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }-1\right) \varphi_{n}\left( x\right) +1\right) ^{n}. \end{align*} But now (\ref{eqphin}) implies that \begin{align*} \left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }-1\right) \varphi_{n} \left( x\right) +1 & =e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\left( 1-e^{\omega\left( a-b\right) }\right) \varphi_{n} \left( x\right) +1\\ & =e^{\omega_{n}\left( b-a\right) }\left( e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-b\right) }-e^{\omega_{n}\left( a-b\right) }\right) +1=e^{\omega_{n}\left( x-a\right) }, \end{align*} so from the preceding equalities we obtain \[ \mathcal{B}_{n}\left( e^{\lambda_{n}x}\right) =e^{\lambda_{n}a}e^{\lambda_{0}\left( x-a\right) }e^{n\omega_{n}\left( x-a\right) }=e^{\lambda_{n}x}. \]

nodes.name: Direct proof of convergence for the special case
nodes.statement: Let $g(x) := x$. Since $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes $1$ and $e^x$, by Korovkin's Theorem it suffices to prove that $\mathcal{B}_{n} g$ converges uniformly to $g$ on $[0,1]$. By (\ref{eqnice}), $\mathcal{B}_{n} g = \varphi_{n}$, so it is enough to show that $\varphi_{n}$ converges uniformly to $g$. Since $\varphi_{n}$ is convex and increasing, its derivative achieves its maximum value over $[0,1]$ at $1$. Now let $g_n$ be the affine function with slope $\varphi_{n}^\prime (1)$ passing thorough the point $(1,1)$. By convexity, $g_n \le \varphi_{n} \le g$, so to obtain the uniform convergence it suffices to show that $\lim_{n\to\infty }\varphi_{n}^\prime (1) = 1$. But this follows immediately by writing explicitly $\varphi_{n}^\prime (1)$, and then using L'Hospital rule, or the Taylor expansion for $e^{1/n}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: For the first assertion, observe that while $f_1$ is trivially $(1, f_1)$-convex, $B_n f_1$ is not. To see why, note that since $B_n f_1 (a) = f_1 (a)$ and $B_n f_1 (b) = f_1 (b)$, the unique function in $\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ interpolating $B_n f_1$ at $a$ and $b$ is $f_1$ itself. If $B_n f_1$ were $(1, f_1)$-convex, we would have $B_n f_1 \le f_1$ on $[a,b]$. But $f_1$ is strictly convex, so by Jensen's inequality (including the equality condition) we have $B_n f_1 (x) > f_1(x)$ for all $x\in (a,b)$. An analogous argument yields the second assertion. Set $h(x) = x$, so both $h$ and $-h$ are convex. Towards a contradiction, suppose that $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ preserves convexity. Then $\mathcal{B}_{n} h \le h$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n}(- h) \le -h$, so $\mathcal{B}_{n} h = h$. Fix $x\in (a,b)$, and note that $f\mapsto \mathcal{B}_{n} f(x)$ is a positive linear functional on $C[a,b]$, defined by a probability measure (since $\mathcal{B}_{n} 1 (x) = 1$). Thus we can once more apply Jensen's inequality, in this case to the strictly concave function $f_1^{-1}$, to conclude that $$x = h(x) = \mathcal{B}_{n} h (x) = \mathcal{B}_{n} (f_1^{-1}\circ f_1) (x) > f_1^{-1} \left( \mathcal{B}_{n} f_1 (x)\right) = f_1^{-1}\left( f_1 (x)\right) = x. $$ Alternatively, we can reach the same conclusion without using Jensen's inequality, by observing that if in addition to fixing $1$ and $f_1$, we have $\mathcal{B}_{n} h = h$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes three linearly independent functions, and thus it must be the identity operator (by \cite[Proposition 3.7]{Mazu09}). So again we have a contradiction.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: Jensen's inequality with its equality case: $B_nf_1>f_1$ inside, and convexity preservation would force $\mathcal{B}_nh=h$, contradicting Jensen for the strictly concave $f_1^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Comparison of (1,f_1)-convexity and convexity
nodes.statement: Let $f_1$ be increasing and strictly convex on $[a,b]$. For increasing functions on $[a,b]$, the condition of $(1, f_1)$-convexity is strictly stronger than convexity. Over the decreasing functions on $[a,b]$, convexity is strictly stronger than $(1, f_1)$-convexity.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
assumptions: $f_1$ be increasing and strictly convex on $[a,b]$
conclusions: For increasing functions on $[a,b]$, the condition of $(1, f_1)$-convexity is strictly stronger than convexity.
Over the decreasing functions on $[a,b]$, convexity is strictly stronger than $(1, f_1)$-convexity.
nodes.statement_short: For convex increasing $f_1$: on increasing functions $(1,f_1)$-convexity is strictly stronger than convexity; on decreasing ones the reverse.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be increasing and $(1, f_1)$-convex on $[a,b]$. Pick $x,y\in [a,b]$ with $x < y$. Since $f(y)\ge f(x)$, the unique interpolant $\psi$ of $f$ at $x$ and $y$ such that $\psi\in\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ must be of the form $\psi = c_0 + c_1 f_1$, with $c_1 \ge 0$. Thus $\psi$ is convex, so the unique interpolant $\phi \in\operatorname{Span}\{1, t\}$ of $\psi$ (or $f$) at $x$ and $y$ satisfies $\phi (t) \ge \psi (t) \ge f(t)$ for all $t\in [x,y]$, whence $f$ is convex. Also, $h(t) := t$ is increasing and convex but not $(1, f_1)$-convex, since $h(f^{-1}_1) = f^{-1}_1$ is strictly concave, cf. Lemma \ref{bepas}. The assertion about decreasing functions is proved by the same type of argument, so we omit it.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: Interpolant in Span$\{1,f_1\}$ of an increasing function has $c_1\ge0$, hence is convex; $h(t)=t$ shows strictness; decreasing case omitted.

nodes.statement: Fix $x\in (a,b)$, and note that $f\mapsto \mathcal{B}_{n} f(x)$ is a positive linear functional on $C[a,b]$, defined by a probability measure (since $\mathcal{B}_{n} 1 (x) = 1$). Thus we can once more apply Jensen's inequality, in this case to the strictly concave function $f_1^{-1}$, to conclude that $$x = h(x) = \mathcal{B}_{n} h (x) = \mathcal{B}_{n} (f_1^{-1}\circ f_1) (x) > f_1^{-1} \left( \mathcal{B}_{n} f_1 (x)\right) = f_1^{-1}\left( f_1 (x)\right) = x. $$
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: Jensen for the strictly concave $f_1^{-1}$ gives $x>x$

nodes.name: Alternative: fixing three independent functions forces the i
nodes.statement: Alternatively, we can reach the same conclusion without using Jensen's inequality, by observing that if in addition to fixing $1$ and $f_1$, we have $\mathcal{B}_{n} h = h$, then $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ fixes three linearly independent functions, and thus it must be the identity operator (by \cite[Proposition 3.7]{Mazu09}). So again we have a contradiction.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: Alternative: fixing three independent functions forces the identity [Mazure]

nodes.name: Take increasing $(1,f_1)$-convex $f$ and points $x<y$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be increasing and $(1, f_1)$-convex on $[a,b]$. Pick $x,y\in [a,b]$ with $x < y$.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: Take increasing $(1,f_1)$-convex $f$ and points $x<y$

nodes.name: The interpolant in Span$\{1,f_1\}$ has $c_1\ge0$
nodes.statement: Since $f(y)\ge f(x)$, the unique interpolant $\psi$ of $f$ at $x$ and $y$ such that $\psi\in\operatorname{Span}\{1, f_1\}$ must be of the form $\psi = c_0 + c_1 f_1$, with $c_1 \ge 0$.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: The interpolant in Span$\{1,f_1\}$ has $c_1\ge0$

nodes.name: Affine interpolant dominates $\psi\ge f$, so $f$ is convex
nodes.statement: Thus $\psi$ is convex, so the unique interpolant $\phi \in\operatorname{Span}\{1, t\}$ of $\psi$ (or $f$) at $x$ and $y$ satisfies $\phi (t) \ge \psi (t) \ge f(t)$ for all $t\in [x,y]$, whence $f$ is convex.
nodes.section: 3 On the generalized Bernstein Operator of Morigi and Neamtu
nodes.statement_short: Affine interpolant dominates $\psi\ge f$, so $f$ is convex

nodes.name: $h(t)=t$ shows the inclusion is strict
nodes.statement: Also, $h(t) := t$ is increasing and convex but not $(1, f_1)$-convex, since $h(f^{-1}_1) = f^{-1}_1$ is strictly concave, cf. Lemma \ref{bepas}.

nodes.statement_short: $h(t)=t$ shows the inclusion is strict

nodes.statement: The assertion about decreasing functions is proved by the same type of argument, so we omit it.
